flashcards.q: What is an access pattern?
flashcards.a: The list of how the app will write and look up data: by which key or condition, how often, and with what guarantees.
flashcards.more: This is the real yardstick for choosing a database. Write five or ten lines like "create order: changes three tables together, 50/second" and it becomes clear which family of database you need. Popularity or a big company's choice does not answer this question.

flashcards.q: Which kind of database should be the default for a new project, and why?
flashcards.a: Relational (PostgreSQL or MySQL). For linked data you get transactions, constraints and SQL for any question, all ready-made.
flashcards.more: Business data is almost always interlinked, and you cannot know at the start which questions will come later. Under that uncertainty a relational database is the lowest-risk choice. Data with no fixed shape does not need anything else either: JSON columns exist.

flashcards.q: What is a key-value database best at, and what can it not do?
flashcards.a: Very fast reads and writes when you know the key: caches, sessions, counters. It cannot search inside values or do joins.
flashcards.more: Think of the token counter at a hospital: say the token number and you get the report at once, but ask for "all diabetic patients' reports" and it cannot help. Redis and Memcached belong to this family. Core business data does not go here; temporary or rebuildable data does.

flashcards.q: When does a document database fit?
flashcards.a: When everything about one thing is read and written together, its shape varies from item to item, and you almost never join across documents.
flashcards.more: A CMS page or a product catalog entry is a good example: it comes in whole and goes out whole. But when the data is interlinked (order, customer, payment) and reports need joins, a document database makes you build those joins in your own code.

flashcards.q: What does a wide-column database (like Cassandra) give you, and what does it take in return?
flashcards.a: It gives huge write capacity spread over many servers. It takes joins and ad-hoc queries: you decide the queries first and shape the tables to match.
flashcards.more: Data is split across servers by a partition key, so writes can scale almost without limit. But you can mostly look things up only by that key. It suits huge workloads with known queries, like chat messages, event logs and sensor data; for an ordinary business app it is extra weight.

flashcards.q: You store orders in Cassandra keyed by customer_id. Can you list all orders of one state?
flashcards.a: Not directly. You can only look up by the key the table was built for, so you would keep a second table (a copy) keyed by state.
flashcards.more: This is the price of wide-column: queries are decided first and each gets its own copy of the data, and every write must update every copy. In relational the same question is one join and a GROUP BY, which is why it is the safer default when the questions are not yet known.

flashcards.q: What are the three traits of time-series data?
flashcards.a: Each row is a timestamp and a measurement; data is only appended, never edited; and queries ask about time windows.
flashcards.more: Server CPU, sensor temperature, share prices: all of this is the same kind of data. A time-series database partitions it by time, compresses old data and deletes it when it expires. TimescaleDB is an extension of PostgreSQL itself, so you can start without adding a separate database.

flashcards.q: When do you need a graph database?
flashcards.a: When the main questions are about relationships many steps deep, such as friends of friends, fraud rings or recommendations, and SQL turns them into deep joins.
flashcards.more: A graph database stores nodes and edges directly, so hopping from one node to its neighbor is cheap. One or two steps of relationship (a customer's orders) work fine in relational. Think of a graph when the depth of the relationships is unknown or large.

flashcards.q: What is the hidden cost of adding a second database?
flashcards.a: Separate backups, monitoring, upgrades and skills, plus the duty of keeping the same fact in agreement in two places.
flashcards.more: The purchase price may be zero, but the running cost is not. Every new database is one more place where the system can break and the data can drift apart. So first check whether the current database can do the job with an index, a cache or an extension.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between a source of truth and derived data?
flashcards.a: The source of truth holds the final facts. Derived data (a cache, a search index) is a copy of it and can be rebuilt from the original if lost.
flashcards.more: When the same fact lives in several places, you must decide which one is the real one. Writes always go to the real one first, and the copies are updated afterwards. If you treat both as "real", one day they will disagree and nobody can say which is right.

flashcards.q: What is normalization, in one sentence?
flashcards.a: Storing each fact once, in its own table, while everything else refers to it by ID (a foreign key).
flashcards.more: The goal is that no fact lives in more than one place, so changing it in one place shows the new value to everyone. That is why the name and phone live in the customer table, and an order holds only the customer_id.

flashcards.q: What is an update anomaly?
flashcards.a: When the same fact is stored in several rows, one is changed and the rest stay stale.
flashcards.more: For example, if a phone number is copied into every order, forgetting a single row when the number changes leaves the same person with two numbers. After that nobody can say which one is right.

flashcards.q: What does a foreign key do?
flashcards.a: It ties a row to a row in another table, and refuses any ID whose row does not exist.
flashcards.more: With an FK you cannot create an order with customer_id = 999 if customer 999 does not exist. Deletes follow the rules too: with RESTRICT the delete is blocked, with CASCADE the related rows are deleted as well.

flashcards.q: Why is a UNIQUE constraint better than a validator check alone?
flashcards.a: Even when two requests arrive together, the database blocks the second one; a validator's "look first" cannot.
flashcards.more: There is a gap between the validator's check and the save. In that gap another request can insert the same value. A UNIQUE index makes the check inside the database as one indivisible step.

flashcards.q: How do you add a CHECK constraint in Doctrine?
flashcards.a: Write addSql('ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (...)') in a migration; Doctrine attributes have no CHECK.
flashcards.more: NOT NULL, UNIQUE and FK come straight from the entity attributes. A business rule like CHECK has to be written in SQL and kept in a migration. That way the rule lives inside the database, whichever code the data comes through.

flashcards.q: When is denormalization justified?
flashcards.a: When the reason is clear: a snapshot that freezes history (an order's price), or a copy for a query measured as slow, with someone responsible for updating it.
flashcards.more: Copying just because you think the join will be slow is a mistake. Measure first and try an index. If you do copy, write down where the original fact lives and who updates the copy and when.

flashcards.q: Why is an order's price copied into its row instead of joining the product's current price?
flashcards.a: So that a later change to the product price does not alter the total of an old invoice.
flashcards.more: This is called a snapshot. The price, tax rate or address at the moment of the order is part of history. The current value and the historical value are different facts, so it is right to keep them in different places.

flashcards.q: What does normalization cost you?
flashcards.a: Reading a record with its related facts needs a JOIN (or a second query). With an index on the foreign key this is usually fast.
flashcards.more: That is the whole price: a few more tables and some joins. It is almost always worth it, because wrong data costs far more than a join. Only when you have measured that a specific join is too slow, and an index does not help, should you consider a copy.

flashcards.q: What is an index, and how does it make queries faster?
flashcards.a: A separate list sorted by a column's values that says where each row is, so the whole table need not be read.
flashcards.more: Like a library catalog: sorted cards take you straight to the shelf. Without an index the database reads every row one by one (a sequential scan).

flashcards.q: What is a B-tree index good for?
flashcards.a: Lookup by value (=), ranges (BETWEEN, >, <) and ORDER BY, because the values are kept sorted.
flashcards.more: Even with 2 million rows the tree is only 3 or 4 levels high, so a lookup finishes in a few steps. The leaves are linked side by side, so a range is one continuous read. But for a middle-of-value search like LIKE '%abc', the sorted tree does not help.

flashcards.q: What is the leftmost prefix rule?
flashcards.a: A composite index works only for queries whose conditions start from the index's leftmost column.
flashcards.more: With an index on (a, b), searching by a, or by a and b together, works. Searching by b alone does not use the index. A phone book sorts by surname and then first name: you cannot look up by first name alone.

flashcards.q: In what order should you arrange the columns of a composite index?
flashcards.a: Columns with equality (=) conditions first, then the range or ORDER BY column.
flashcards.more: For WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC, the right index is (customer_id, created_at). With the equality column first, the remaining columns are sorted inside it, so no separate sort is needed.

flashcards.q: What does Seq Scan in EXPLAIN tell you?
flashcards.a: The database read the whole table. On a big table it usually means an index is missing or not being used.
flashcards.more: A big number in Rows Removed by Filter shows how many rows were read and discarded. On a small table Seq Scan is fine: the database chose it on purpose because it is cheap. Always test with production-sized data.

flashcards.q: What is a covering index?
flashcards.a: An index that holds every column the query needs, so the real table rows are never touched (Index Only Scan).
flashcards.more: In PostgreSQL, INCLUDE (col) lets you keep extra columns in the leaf. Reads get faster, but the index grows and writes cost more. So use it only for very frequent queries.

flashcards.q: What is a partial index, and when is it useful?
flashcards.a: An index over only some rows, chosen by a WHERE condition (such as status = pending). It stays small and does not slow writes of the other rows.
flashcards.more: When most rows in a table are "finished" and queries care only about the active ones, an index over the whole table is a waste. In Doctrine, #[ORM\Index(options: ['where' => '...'])] creates a partial index on PostgreSQL. A query uses it only when it repeats the same WHERE condition.

flashcards.q: What is the cost of having many indexes?
flashcards.a: Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must update every index, so writes get slower and disk use grows.
flashcards.more: It is like adding a card to every catalog when a new book arrives. An index that no query uses only adds write cost. In PostgreSQL, look at pg_stat_user_indexes for indexes with idx_scan = 0 and drop them.

flashcards.q: What is a storage engine?
flashcards.a: The part of a database that decides how data is written to and read from disk.
flashcards.more: The SQL can be the same while the engine inside differs. The engine decides which jobs are fast and which are slow: writes, reads, range queries or big data. So when choosing a database you look at the engine, not only the features.

flashcards.q: What does a B-tree engine do on a write, and what follows from it?
flashcards.a: It finds the right sorted page and puts the data there. Reads are fast, but writing into scattered pages means random writes.
flashcards.more: A full page splits in two. This is the price of fast reads: the data is always sorted, so you walk down the tree and land right on it. It is the engine of PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB and SQLite.

flashcards.q: Why is an LSM-tree fast at writes?
flashcards.a: Writes gather in memory and are appended to the end of the disk, which is sequential; no scattered pages need changing.
flashcards.more: In a Log-Structured Merge-tree, a disk file never changes once written. Compaction later merges and sorts them in the background. In return, a read may have to check several files.

flashcards.q: What is the WAL, and why is it needed?
flashcards.a: Writing a change to a sequential log before applying it in its real place; after a crash you read it to restore the data.
flashcards.more: Appending to a WAL is cheap, and once it has reached the disk it is safe to say "done". When a server crashes, the data in memory is lost, but it is rebuilt from the WAL. PostgreSQL, MySQL and Cassandra all use a WAL or an equivalent log.

flashcards.q: What does compaction do?
flashcards.a: It merges an LSM's many sorted files into one new file, leaving out old values and deleted rows.
flashcards.more: Without compaction, files would keep piling up and a read would have to check many of them. In the background it eats disk and CPU, so under extreme write load the database can suddenly slow down. That is the main price of an LSM.

flashcards.q: What is write amplification?
flashcards.a: The ratio of how many times the disk is really written for one write: WAL, files and compaction together.
flashcards.more: The higher the amplification, the more disk wear and the lower the speed. In a B-tree, even a small change rewrites a whole page. In an LSM, the same data is written to new files several times during compaction. Both engines have it, in different forms.

flashcards.q: Which databases are B-tree, and which are LSM?
flashcards.a: B-tree: PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQLite. LSM: Cassandra, ScyllaDB, RocksDB, HBase.
flashcards.more: For an ordinary business app, a B-tree-based relational database is the default. When you have huge continuous writes and known queries (logs, sensors, chat), you can consider an LSM-based database.

flashcards.q: Why is committing 1,000 rows one by one slow, and what is the first fix?
flashcards.a: Each commit waits for its own disk flush (about 5 ms each, 5 s in total). Put the rows in one transaction, in chunks of about 1,000.
flashcards.more: Batching keeps full durability: when the transaction commits, the data is safely on disk. Only after batching has proved too slow should you consider synchronous_commit = off, and only for data you can afford to lose.

flashcards.q: What are the three main limits of an auto-increment ID?
flashcards.a: It can be guessed, it leaks business size, and IDs collide when generated in more than one database.
flashcards.more: It has strengths too: it is small (8 bytes), appended to the end of the index, and made by the database itself. For an app that never shows IDs outside and has a single database, it is the simplest and best choice.

flashcards.q: What is UUIDv4, and what is its main weakness?
flashcards.a: A 16-byte ID with 122 random bits. It can be made anywhere, but being unordered it scatters across a B-tree index.
flashcards.more: Each new row lands on any page of the tree, so pages split and cache misses go up. You will not notice on a small table; on a big one inserts slow down.

flashcards.q: What is UUIDv7, and why is it better than v4?
flashcards.a: 48 bits of millisecond time up front and the rest random. It sorts by time, so it is appended at the end of the index.
flashcards.more: It keeps every UUID benefit (made anywhere, hard to guess) and also gives an order that suits a B-tree. In Symfony it is Uuid::v7(). For a new project that wants UUIDs, this is the default choice.

flashcards.q: What are the three parts of a Snowflake ID?
flashcards.a: 41 bits of time (ms), 10 bits of machine id and 12 bits of counter: 64 bits in all, which fits in a bigint.
flashcards.more: Each machine can make 4096 IDs per millisecond. The benefits: small (8 bytes) and sorted by time. The price: every server needs a distinct machine id, and you must be careful if the clock moves backwards.

flashcards.q: How are ULID and UUIDv7 alike and different?
flashcards.a: Both are 48 bits of time plus a random part. A ULID is written as 26 base32 characters; a UUIDv7 uses the standard UUID format.
flashcards.more: UUIDv7 is a standard (RFC 9562), so it goes straight into a database's native uuid type. A ULID is also 128 bits, and Symfony Uid has Ulid and UlidType. Both are good; UUIDv7 has more tool support.

flashcards.q: How do you make an entity's ID a UUIDv7 in Symfony?
flashcards.a: Give the field UuidType::NAME and set $this->id = Uuid::v7() in the constructor.
flashcards.more: When you make the ID yourself you do not need GeneratedValue, and the ID is known before flush. With Requirement::UUID_V7 on the route, an ID in the wrong format gets a 404 before it enters the controller.

flashcards.q: Does using a UUID prevent IDOR?
flashcards.a: No. IDs can leak. Checking ownership (a voter) on every request is the real protection.
flashcards.more: IDOR means seeing someone else's data by changing an ID. A UUID makes guessing hard, but IDs can escape through shared links, logs or browser history. Without an authorization check, everything is then open.

flashcards.q: What is leader/follower replication?
flashcards.a: One node (the leader) takes all the writes and sends the changes to the followers; the followers keep copies and serve read requests.
flashcards.more: Because writes go only to the leader, their order stays consistent. Followers spread the read load, and if the leader dies, one follower can become the new leader. "Primary/replica" is another name for the same idea.

flashcards.q: Does replication increase write capacity?
flashcards.a: No. Writes still go to a single leader. Replication increases read capacity and the chance of surviving a failure.
flashcards.more: When the write load goes beyond one server, you have to split the data, which is sharding. Before that, consider indexes, caching, better queries and a bigger server.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between sync and async replication?
flashcards.a: With async, the leader commits without waiting for followers (fast, but a crash can lose data). With sync, it waits (safe, but slow).
flashcards.more: In PostgreSQL, synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (a, b)' makes a commit succeed as soon as any one follower confirms. Writes do not stop even if one follower dies.

flashcards.q: What is replication lag?
flashcards.a: The time a change on the leader takes to reach a follower. With async it may be small, but it is never zero.
flashcards.more: Lag grows with heavy writes, network delay or a slow follower. It is important to measure it (pg_stat_replication) and alert when it passes a limit; otherwise users keep seeing stale data.

flashcards.q: What is read-your-own-writes?
flashcards.a: The guarantee that a user sees what they have just written in their next read. Reading from a follower can break it.
flashcards.more: The fix: read from the leader for a short time after a write (or for the related reads), or check how far the follower has got before reading. In Doctrine, ensureConnectedToPrimary() does this.

flashcards.q: How do you set up replicas in Doctrine?
flashcards.a: Keep the main url (the primary) in doctrine.yaml and add replicas: beneath it; DoctrineBundle then uses PrimaryReadReplicaConnection.
flashcards.more: After a write or the start of a transaction, every other query in that request goes to the primary. So within one request you see your own writes; the problem is in the next request, which is why you need a sticky mechanism.

flashcards.q: What is split brain, and how do you prevent it?
flashcards.a: Two nodes both believing they are the leader and taking writes. Prevent it by fencing the old leader so it cannot write.
flashcards.more: Two leaders means two different truths, which are very hard and sometimes impossible to merge later. So in a failover you first stop the old one and only then promote the new leader. Patroni or a managed service does this properly.

flashcards.q: Is a follower a backup?
flashcards.a: No. Every change reaches the followers, including a wrong DELETE or DROP. A backup keeps older states you can go back to.
flashcards.more: Replication protects you from a dead machine, not from a human mistake or a bad deploy, because the mistake is copied within moments. You still need real backups, with point-in-time recovery if the data matters.

flashcards.q: How do you stop a user seeing stale data on the request right after a write?
flashcards.a: Remember the write (for example in the session) and send that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds, longer than the usual lag.
flashcards.more: Doctrine switches to the primary only inside the request that wrote. A small listener that calls ensureConnectedToPrimary() while `primary_until` is in the future carries the guarantee into the next requests. The price is a little less read offloading; the window must be longer than your real lag.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between partitioning and sharding?
flashcards.a: Partitioning splits a table into smaller pieces, usually on one server. Sharding puts those pieces on separate servers.
flashcards.more: Partitioning is simple and barely touches the app: it makes archiving old data and some queries faster. Sharding scales write capacity across servers, but the app has to know where the data lives.

flashcards.q: What should you try before sharding?
flashcards.a: Fix indexes and queries, add a cache, buy a bigger server, add read replicas, then partition and archive.
flashcards.more: Every one of these steps is cheaper and less risky than sharding. Most apps run for years on them. You only shard when a single server's write limit is truly exceeded.

flashcards.q: What is a shard key?
flashcards.a: The column whose value decides which shard a row lives on, such as customer_id.
flashcards.more: The router computes the shard from that value, and the same key always lands on the same shard. With the right key, most queries finish on a single shard.

flashcards.q: What makes a good shard key?
flashcards.a: Many distinct values, an even spread of load, presence in most queries, and a value that never changes.
flashcards.more: customer_id is often a good fit: many values, even spread, and it appears in queries. Country or status is bad because it has few values and a lopsided spread. Dates are risky too: all new data piles onto one shard.

flashcards.q: What is a hot shard and what causes it?
flashcards.a: A shard that carries far more load than the rest. Causes: a bad shard key (country, date) or one huge user.
flashcards.more: When one shard is slow, every query that goes there is slow while the other shards sit idle, so adding servers doesn't help. The fixes: a better key, a separate shard for big tenants, or hashing the key.

flashcards.q: What is scatter-gather and why is it slow?
flashcards.a: Sending a query without the shard key to every shard and merging the results. The slowest shard sets the time for the whole query.
flashcards.more: The cost grows with every shard you add, and one slow shard slows everything. Joins and unique constraints also stop working across shards. That is why you design the split around your access patterns.

flashcards.q: Why do virtual buckets make resharding easier?
flashcards.a: A key maps to one of about 1024 buckets, and each bucket maps to a shard. Adding shards changes only the bucket-to-shard map, not the hash.
flashcards.more: With plain hash % N, going from 4 to 5 shards moves 4 rows in 5. With buckets you move only about a fifth, one bucket at a time, so resharding can happen step by step.

flashcards.q: You add a 5th shard to 4. How many rows move with hash % N, and with 1024 buckets?
flashcards.a: About 80% with hash % N (4 of every 5 rows change shard). About 20% with buckets, moved one bucket at a time.
flashcards.more: With buckets the hash never changes. A map says which shard owns each of the 1024 buckets, and you hand about 205 of them to the new shard. For each one: dual write, copy, verify, flip the map, clean up.

flashcards.q: What is a consistency model?
flashcards.a: The rules or guarantees about who sees what, and when, when there are several copies of the data.
flashcards.more: With only one copy there is nothing to ask. Once replication, caches or shards add copies, the copies are not always identical. A model decides exactly how much mismatch you tolerate.

flashcards.q: What does strong consistency give you, and what does it cost?
flashcards.a: After a write finishes, everyone sees the latest value, as if there were one copy. It costs more delay and more risk of failure.
flashcards.more: Writes must wait for all copies to agree, so they are slower. If a copy can't be reached, reads or writes may stall. Use it only for things like money and stock.

flashcards.q: What is eventual consistency?
flashcards.a: If no new writes arrive, all copies converge on the same value after a while. In between, copies may show different values.
flashcards.more: It is the fastest and most available rule, because nobody waits. It works well for likes, view counts and feeds. It does not work for money.

flashcards.q: What is read-your-writes, and how do you provide it?
flashcards.a: A user sees their own write on their next read. Read from the primary after a write, or check that the replica has caught up.
flashcards.more: Others seeing the change a little late is harmless, so this is a cheap rule. In PostgreSQL, note pg_current_wal_lsn() after the write, then check that the replica's pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() is at or past it.

flashcards.q: What are monotonic reads?
flashcards.a: Once you have seen newer data, later reads never show older data: time doesn't go backwards.
flashcards.more: It breaks when likes or comments drop on a refresh. The easy fix is to always send the user to the same replica, since a single replica never goes back in time.

flashcards.q: What is causal consistency?
flashcards.a: An event that depends on another is seen after it: the question comes before the answer.
flashcards.more: A single-leader replica keeps write order, but with separate shards or multi-leader the answer can arrive first. The fix is to store a pointer to the cause on the reply and not show the reply until that cause is readable.

flashcards.q: How can an app give causal order when a question and its answer live on different shards?
flashcards.a: Store a pointer to the cause on the answer (the question shard's log position). Before showing the answer, check the cause is readable, else read it from the primary.
flashcards.more: Hiding orphan replies in the browser is not enough, because emails and API clients still see them. The price is one extra column, one cheap query per reply, and some primary reads while the replica lags. A single-leader table keeps order by itself and needs none of this.

flashcards.q: Which consistency rules fit a balance and a like count?
flashcards.a: Balance: strong (read from the primary). Like count: eventual is enough.
flashcards.more: The deciding question: could stale data lead to a wrong decision about money, stock or security? If yes, strong. If not, use the loosest rule that doesn't confuse the user.

flashcards.q: What is the N+1 query problem?
flashcards.a: One query for the list, then one more for each of the list's N rows: N+1 queries in all.
flashcards.more: For example, on a 50-order page, fetching each order's customer name in a separate query runs 51 queries. Each query is fast, but every one pays for a round trip to the database. More rows means more queries, so the page slows down gradually.

flashcards.q: What does lazy loading mean in Doctrine?
flashcards.a: A proxy stands in for the related entity, and a separate query runs the first time you ask for its data.
flashcards.more: When Doctrine loads an order, it doesn't bring the customer along. It puts in a shell (a proxy) that knows only the id. Calling `getName()` makes the proxy run a `SELECT`. For one entity that saves work, but inside a loop it fires one query per iteration and creates N+1.

flashcards.q: Why doesn't the slow query log catch N+1?
flashcards.a: Each query is fast on its own. What is slow is their total number in one request.
flashcards.more: The slow query log records only queries that take a long time by themselves. Each N+1 query may finish in 1 ms, yet 500 of them add up to half a second. So measure "queries per request" with the Symfony Profiler, an APM tool or a test's query count.

flashcards.q: How can a test stop N+1 from coming back?
flashcards.a: In a functional test, enable the profiler and assert that the `db` collector's `getQueryCount()` stays under a limit.
flashcards.more: Call `$client->enableProfiler()`, send the request, then read the number from `$client->getProfile()->getCollector('db')->getQueryCount()`. Put enough rows in the fixture (say 50), otherwise the count looks small even with N+1. If the limit is exceeded, the test fails.

flashcards.q: What two things does a fetch join in Doctrine's QueryBuilder need?
flashcards.a: `join()` (or `leftJoin()`) and `addSelect()`. Without the second, the joined entity stays a proxy.
flashcards.more: `join()` only adds a JOIN to the SQL, which helps with filtering or sorting. Only `addSelect('c')` brings the joined entity's columns into the SELECT so Doctrine builds it from the same query. Many people write only `join()` and think N+1 is solved. It isn't.

flashcards.q: What is the benefit of a DTO instead of full entities on a list page?
flashcards.a: Only the needed columns come back, objects are cheap to build, and Doctrine doesn't have to track changes on all those entities.
flashcards.more: In DQL, `SELECT NEW App\Dto\OrderRow(o.id, c.name, …)` returns the results directly as small readonly objects. It suits any page that only displays data: lists, reports, API responses. If you need to change and save, you still need the entity.

flashcards.q: Why is batch loading better than a fetch join for to-many collections?
flashcards.a: A JOIN multiplies the rows and repeats the parent's columns. Batch loading loads every collection in a second `IN (…)` query.
flashcards.more: With 50 orders and 4 items each, a JOIN returns 200 rows, each carrying all the order columns. Joining two collections together multiplies the rows (a cartesian product). With batch loading, the first query fetches the orders and the second all the items: always 2 queries, no repetition.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong with `setMaxResults(20)` on a collection fetch join?
flashcards.a: LIMIT applies to SQL rows, not entities, so you get fewer than 20 entities, and the last one's collection may be incomplete.
flashcards.more: After the JOIN, one order becomes many rows. With 4 items per order, `LIMIT 20` gives only 5 orders. Doctrine raises no error, so the mistake slips past unnoticed. The fix: paginate the main entity first, then load the collection.

flashcards.q: How does Doctrine's Paginator keep pages correct with a collection join?
flashcards.a: It first uses LIMIT to pick just the main entity ids, then loads those entities with their collections via `WHERE id IN (…)`.
flashcards.more: When you write `new Paginator($query, fetchJoinCollection: true)`, Doctrine splits your one query in two: one that selects the ids, then one for the full data. Calling `count()` runs a third, COUNT query. That is two or three queries, but the page gets exactly as many entities as you asked for.

flashcards.q: What is OLTP?
flashcards.a: A huge number of small, fast transactions (orders, payments, logins), where each query touches a few rows.
flashcards.more: Online Transaction Processing is the app's everyday database. Responses are needed within milliseconds. Finding rows through an index, small writes and short transactions are its hallmarks.

flashcards.q: What is OLAP?
flashcards.a: Fewer but heavy queries that total, average or trend across hundreds of thousands to millions of rows.
flashcards.more: Online Analytical Processing serves business questions such as "How much did each category sell last year?" These queries read a few columns but from a great many rows, which is why column-oriented storage is faster for them.

flashcards.q: Why shouldn't reports run on the transactional database?
flashcards.a: A heavy scan hogs CPU, memory and disk, and slows customers' small queries.
flashcards.more: The two jobs share one server's resources. If a report runs for a few minutes, order saves slow down, requests time out and customers leave. So reports need a separate copy.

flashcards.q: What is derived data?
flashcards.a: A copy or summary built from the original data (the source of truth), which you can rebuild if it is lost.
flashcards.more: Caches, search indexes, materialized views and warehouse tables are all derived data. They are good for reading, but they are not the truth. When there is a mismatch, you trust the source of truth.

flashcards.q: How does a materialized view differ from a plain view?
flashcards.a: A plain view runs its query every time; a materialized view stores the result on disk and changes when you refresh it.
flashcards.more: Because the result is stored, you can index it and reads are very fast. The price is that the data stays old until the next refresh. In PostgreSQL, `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` updates it without blocking reads, but it needs a unique index.

flashcards.q: What is change data capture (CDC)?
flashcards.a: Reading the database's transaction log (such as the WAL) and sending every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE to another system as an event.
flashcards.more: The app's code doesn't change, because the true list of changes is already in the database's log. Debezium is a popular tool for it. It avoids the dual-write gap, and copies receive the changes in order. It is not free: see the cost card.

flashcards.q: Why is a dual write dangerous?
flashcards.a: If one app writes to two places, one write can succeed and the other fail, and the two quietly drift apart.
flashcards.more: The two writes are not in a single transaction, so there is no guarantee that both succeed or both fail. The fix: write in one place and build the other copies with CDC or an outbox.

flashcards.q: What does a materialized view still cost the primary, and what can it not do?
flashcards.a: Each refresh recomputes everything on the primary, and the view answers only the one question it was built for.
flashcards.more: On 50 million orders a refresh might mean minutes of heavy work, and it grows with the table. A new question, such as revenue by city per day, needs a new view or a finer summary table. Questions that keep changing belong in a warehouse.

flashcards.q: How can a summary table be refreshed more cheaply than a materialized view?
flashcards.a: Each night, add only yesterday's totals with an upsert (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`). Months and years are sums of the daily rows.
flashcards.more: The nightly query reads one day of orders through an index on created_at, so the work no longer grows with the whole table. Running it twice for the same day just overwrites the row, so a retry is safe.

flashcards.q: What are the costs and risks of CDC?
flashcards.a: Extra machinery (Debezium and a broker), an initial snapshot of old rows, and WAL that piles up on the primary if the tool stops reading.
flashcards.more: PostgreSQL keeps WAL files until the replication slot has read them. A CDC tool that is down for a weekend can fill the primary's disk, so alert on slot lag. Also set `wal_level = logical` and plan the first snapshot for a quiet hour.

flashcards.q: What is wrong with storing photos in a database BLOB column?
flashcards.a: The database bloats, backups become huge, and every photo read adds load on the database.
flashcards.more: A database is good at complex queries and small rows, not large binaries. BLOBs also raise cache and replication costs. Keep the photo in object storage and only the key in the database.

flashcards.q: When does saving uploads on the server's local disk break?
flashcards.a: When you have more than one server or container, and when a deploy wipes the files.
flashcards.more: Every server has its own disk. If the load balancer sends a request to a different server, the file isn't there. Rebuilding a container also erases the files on its disk. To keep servers stateless, keep files outside them.

flashcards.q: What is a "key" in object storage?
flashcards.a: The unique path-like name of a file (such as `avatars/uuid.jpg`) that you use to find it in storage.
flashcards.more: The server builds the key itself, usually with a UUID, so two people's files never collide on a name. Storing the key rather than the URL in the database means the data stays valid when the domain or CDN changes.

flashcards.q: What is Flysystem used for in Symfony?
flashcards.a: It gives one API for local disk, S3, GCS and more; changing storage means changing only config.
flashcards.more: `FilesystemOperator`'s `write`, `writeStream`, `read` and `delete` stay the same in your code. The usual pattern is the local adapter in development and the aws adapter in production. For large files use `writeStream` so you don't run out of RAM.

flashcards.q: What is a presigned URL?
flashcards.a: A time-limited URL signed by the server, with which a client can put or read a file in storage directly.
flashcards.more: The signature covers the key, the HTTP method and the expiry; if any of those change, storage rejects it. When it expires, the URL stops working. That way you grant access without handing the client the storage credentials. It cannot limit the file size: for that you need a presigned POST.

flashcards.q: Why must the server run a confirm step after an upload?
flashcards.a: It doesn't trust the client: it checks that the file exists and that its size and type are right, and only then saves the key.
flashcards.more: A client can claim "done" without uploading anything, or upload a file of a different size. The server uses `headObject` to check the size and content type. If everything matches, it moves the database record from `pending` to `uploaded`.

flashcards.q: How do you cap the size of a direct upload to object storage?
flashcards.a: Use a presigned POST with a `content-length-range` condition. Storage then refuses any body outside that range.
flashcards.more: A presigned PUT can't limit size, because the content length isn't part of its signature. With the PHP SDK, `PostObjectV4` builds the signed form fields; the browser sends them as `FormData` with the file as the last field. Also check the size at confirm, as a second line of defense.

flashcards.q: How do you stop abandoned uploads piling up in the bucket?
flashcards.a: Save a `pending` row when you mint the URL, flip it to `uploaded` at confirm, and delete rows still pending after an hour, with their objects.
flashcards.more: Without the pending row nobody knows an orphan object exists. A Symfony Scheduler job runs hourly. For abandoned multipart uploads add a bucket lifecycle rule that aborts them after about 7 days.

flashcards.q: When do you need multipart upload, and how does it work?
flashcards.a: For big files (100 MB+): the file is cut into parts, each sent to its own URL, and finally all the parts are stitched together.
flashcards.more: The steps: `CreateMultipartUpload` (uploadId), a presigned `UploadPart` per part, collect the ETags, and finally `CompleteMultipartUpload`. If a part fails, you resend only that one. Add a lifecycle rule so abandoned parts don't keep costing you.

flashcards.q: How does a multipart upload resume after a crash or refresh?
flashcards.a: Keep the uploadId, ask storage for its parts with `ListParts`, skip those, send only the missing ones, then complete from storage's list.
flashcards.more: The page saves the uploadId in `localStorage`, and the user picks the same file again. Never complete from a list of ETags the browser kept: the server reads `ListParts` itself and checks that the part count is what it expects.

flashcards.q: What is schema evolution?
flashcards.a: Changing the shape of data (its fields) over time so that old and new readers and writers keep working together.
flashcards.more: APIs, queue messages and files all follow a schema. But the parties don't all deploy at once. So a change has to be made in a way that nobody breaks in between.

flashcards.q: Why is Protobuf smaller than JSON?
flashcards.a: It sends a small number instead of the field name, and writes numbers in a compact binary form.
flashcards.more: JSON writes `"total_amount"` into every message. Protobuf sends only the field number and the value. The price is that you need tooling to read it, and both sides must have the schema file.

flashcards.q: In Protobuf, which is safe to change: a field's name or its number?
flashcards.a: The name is safe, the number is not. Only numbers go over the wire, so changing one makes old data read as the wrong field.
flashcards.more: The name only matters in code; the number is the data's identity. So never change or reuse a number in a .proto file. When you remove a field, mark it `reserved`.

flashcards.q: What is the safe rule for adding a new field?
flashcards.a: Make it optional or give it a default, so a reader doesn't break when an old sender's message lacks it.
flashcards.more: In PHP, a default on a constructor parameter (`string $currency = 'USD'`) lets you read old messages still in the queue. If you want a required field, add it as optional first, and make it required once everyone sends it.

flashcards.q: What are the steps for safely renaming a field?
flashcards.a: Add the field under the new name, send both for a while, then remove the old one once everyone reads the new one.
flashcards.more: A rename is really one add and one remove. The period when you send both names bridges old and new readers. Before removing, check the logs to confirm nobody still reads the old one.

flashcards.q: What is a tolerant reader?
flashcards.a: A reader that ignores fields it doesn't recognize and assumes defaults for fields that are missing.
flashcards.more: A strict reader breaks the moment a sender adds a field. Read only what you need and ignore the rest. That leaves the sender free to evolve.

flashcards.q: What does a schema registry do?
flashcards.a: It stores every schema version and checks compatibility before a new schema is accepted, so breaking schemas are stopped.
flashcards.more: Messages carry a small schema id rather than the whole schema; the consumer uses it to fetch the schema from the registry. The rules can be set to BACKWARD, FORWARD or FULL mode.

flashcards.q: About how big is one small order message in JSON, Protobuf and Avro?
flashcards.a: Roughly 54 bytes in JSON, 11 in Protobuf and 9 in Avro. The binary formats skip the field names.
flashcards.more: The example is order_id 9001, total_amount 2500, currency USD. JSON repeats every field name in every message. At 1,000 messages a second that is about 54 KB against 11 KB. For a browser-facing API the readability of JSON usually wins anyway; measure before switching.

flashcards.q: Why does a reused Protobuf field number go unnoticed?
flashcards.a: If the new field has the same kind of type, old data parses without error and is simply read with the new meaning.
flashcards.more: Old phone numbers (strings in field 4) read as a new string `coupon_code` in field 4 look like valid data. Writing `reserved 4;` makes the compiler refuse the reuse before it ships.

flashcards.q: What does zero-downtime migration mean?
flashcards.a: The site stays up during the schema change, and both old and new code keep working.
flashcards.more: There are two goals: avoid long locks, and cope with the period during a deploy when old and new code run side by side. As a result, a migration is usually split into several small, separate releases.

flashcards.q: Why can a 40-second ALTER freeze a site that serves 100 requests a second?
flashcards.a: Every query on the table queues behind the lock: 4,000 of them in 40 seconds, enough to fill a pool of 50 connections within a second.
flashcards.more: Once the connection pool is full, even pages that never touch that table can't get a connection. CPU stays low because everything is waiting, not working. That is why a `lock_timeout` matters: it makes the ALTER give up instead of the site.

flashcards.q: What is expand-migrate-contract?
flashcards.a: A three-phase safe change: add the new structure, move data and code across, then delete the old one.
flashcards.more: To rename a column: add a new column (expand), write to both and backfill, then read from the new one (migrate), and finally drop the old column (contract). Each step is its own deploy, so at every moment both old and new code work.

flashcards.q: Why is renaming a column and changing code in one release dangerous?
flashcards.a: During the deploy, some servers still run old code that looks for the old column name, which no longer exists.
flashcards.more: In a rolling deploy, old and new code run side by side for a while. It's impossible to change the migration and the code at the same instant. So keep the schema in a state that works for both versions.

flashcards.q: What must you do to run `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` in a Doctrine Migration?
flashcards.a: Return `false` from `isTransactional()`, because PostgreSQL won't let that command run inside a transaction.
flashcards.more: `CONCURRENTLY` builds the index without locking the table, but takes longer. If it fails it leaves an INVALID index behind; drop it with `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and build it again. Keep such migrations small, because without a transaction a failure halfway can't be rolled back.

flashcards.q: What is the benefit of setting `lock_timeout` in a migration?
flashcards.a: If it can't get the lock, the migration fails by itself after a short wait, so queries don't pile up behind it and take the site down.
flashcards.more: `SET lock_timeout = '3s'` means it never waits more than 3 seconds for a lock. The migration fails, but the site keeps running. You can try again during a quiet period.

flashcards.q: How do you backfill a big table?
flashcards.a: In small batches (say 1,000 rows), advancing by `id`, with pauses between them, in a command you can safely rerun.
flashcards.more: A single `UPDATE` over millions of rows creates a long lock and a huge transaction. Batching keeps each lock short: about 0.06 s per 1,000 rows instead of 10 minutes for the whole table. The price is a longer total run, around 27 minutes for 10 million rows. An `IS NULL` condition makes reruns safe. Measure replica lag to tune the speed.

flashcards.q: What does `ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID` do?
flashcards.a: It enforces the constraint on new writes right away, but postpones checking existing rows. That keeps the lock short.
flashcards.more: Running `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` afterwards checks the existing rows, and reads and writes continue meanwhile. This works for foreign keys and CHECK constraints. In PostgreSQL 12+, a valid CHECK lets `SET NOT NULL` skip the scan.

flashcards.q: How do you add a foreign key on a huge table without blocking writes?
flashcards.a: Add it with `NOT VALID` first, then run `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` as a separate statement while traffic carries on.
flashcards.more: A plain `ADD FOREIGN KEY` checks every existing row while holding a lock. With `NOT VALID` only new writes are checked at first, so the lock is brief, and `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT` then checks the old rows under a weaker lock.

flashcards.q: What is an audit trail?
flashcards.a: An add-only list of who changed what and when, including the old and new values.
flashcards.more: Rows are only ever added to an audit table; they are never changed or deleted. It lets you settle disputes with evidence, repair mistakes, and meet legal obligations.

flashcards.q: Why is the audit log written in the same transaction as the main change?
flashcards.a: So the change and its history succeed or fail together; if one slips through alone, the history has a gap or false data.
flashcards.more: In Doctrine, use `$em->wrapInTransaction()`. In a separate transaction, there would be a window where the change succeeds but the audit write fails. To catch writes made outside the app, a database trigger is safest.

flashcards.q: How do you stop old invoices changing when a product's price changes?
flashcards.a: Copy the price onto the order line (`unit_price`) at the time of sale, and never join back to `products.price` for invoices.
flashcards.more: The invoice then rests on its own row, so a later UPDATE of the product cannot touch it. The price of this simplicity: it only knows prices that were actually sold. To answer "what was the price on 10 February?" for any product, use effective dating.

flashcards.q: What is effective dating?
flashcards.a: Storing `valid_from` and `valid_to` with each value, so you can say which value was valid on any date.
flashcards.more: Instead of editing a row, you close the old row's `valid_to` and open a new row. An empty `valid_to` means still in force. That gives you both past prices and prices scheduled for the future.

flashcards.q: How do you stop time ranges from overlapping in PostgreSQL?
flashcards.a: With the constraint `EXCLUDE USING gist (product_id WITH =, tstzrange(valid_from, valid_to) WITH &&)`.
flashcards.more: It says that no two rows may have the same `product_id` and overlapping time ranges. It needs the `btree_gist` extension. Even if the application code has a bug, the database won't accept the bad data.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between soft delete and hard delete?
flashcards.a: Soft delete keeps the row and sets `deleted_at`; hard delete really removes the row.
flashcards.more: Soft delete lets you undo accidental deletes and keep history, but personal data stays and a forgotten filter exposes deleted rows. For privacy requests or expired data, you eventually need a hard delete.

flashcards.q: Why does an email unique constraint break with soft delete?
flashcards.a: The deleted row still holds the email, so a new row with the same email can't be inserted.
flashcards.more: The fix is a partial unique index instead of a plain `UNIQUE (email)`: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ... ON users (lower(email)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`. Then uniqueness applies only among live rows.

flashcards.q: How do you add `deleted_at IS NULL` to every query in Doctrine?
flashcards.a: Write an `SQLFilter` and enable it in `doctrine.yaml`; Doctrine then adds the condition to every WHERE itself.
flashcards.more: Return `%s.deleted_at IS NULL` from `addFilterConstraint()`. The filter doesn't apply to native SQL or DBAL queries, where you must write it by hand. Forgetting it in report queries is a common source of mistakes.

flashcards.q: What does data lifecycle mean?
flashcards.a: The whole journey of data: collection, use, storage, archiving and finally deletion.
flashcards.more: Many people think only about collecting data, never about deleting it. As a result, data piles up for years for no reason. Think on the day you collect it: why you keep it, for how long, and what happens at the end.

flashcards.q: Where is one user's data usually spread?
flashcards.a: Besides the main table: logs, search indexes, analytics or a warehouse, caches, backups and third-party services.
flashcards.more: Deleting the main table doesn't delete these copies. So a "delete me" request needs a list of every copy. A data map made in advance makes deletion much easier.

flashcards.q: What is a retention policy?
flashcards.a: A written rule for each kind of data: why you keep it, how long, and whether you delete or archive it afterwards.
flashcards.more: Login logs 90 days, invoices 7 years by law, and so on. The numbers come from law and business needs. Don't leave the policy on paper; enforce it with config and a job.

flashcards.q: What is the data minimization principle?
flashcards.a: Collect and keep only the information you really need to provide the service.
flashcards.more: Data you never collected can't leak and never has to be deleted. Before adding a field to a form, ask whether you can do without it. Checking "is the user 18 or over" is enough; you don't need the full date of birth.

flashcards.q: How should a purge job run?
flashcards.a: On a schedule through the Scheduler, in small batches, with the retention period in config, logging how many rows it deleted.
flashcards.more: Delete about 5,000 rows per batch, and repeat while full batches keep coming. On big tables, partitioning and dropping an old partition is even faster. Watching the counts helps you spot anything unusual.

flashcards.q: What is the correct order for archive-then-delete?
flashcards.a: Select, write to the archive, verify row counts and checksums, and only then delete from the main table.
flashcards.more: Skip verification and a failed archive write still results in deleted data, leaving nothing at all. Keep archives in cheap object storage, in year-month folders, so you can find them later.

flashcards.q: Why must the list of erased users be kept outside the database you back up?
flashcards.a: A restore rolls the whole database back, so a list inside it would lose the newest erasures along with the data they should re-delete.
flashcards.more: Say the backup is from last night and the crash is today. Anyone erased this morning is back after the restore, and an `erasure_log` table in the same database is back to last night's state too, so it no longer lists them. A list kept in a separate small database or an append-only file survives the restore, and you re-anonymize everyone on it.

flashcards.q: What happens to a user's order rows when they say "delete my data"?
flashcards.a: Usually the rows stay, but the name, email, phone and address are anonymized.
flashcards.more: Accounting and tax law require order records to be kept for several years. Removing the personal data keeps the legal record while making the person unidentifiable. Data like photos, files and marketing lists gets deleted outright.

flashcards.q: What is a data warehouse?
flashcards.a: A separate database for clean, structured data, built for analysis and reporting.
flashcards.more: Data is cleaned and arranged into tables before being stored, so SQL reports are fast and reliable. Examples: BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift. Data is copied here from the transactional databases.

flashcards.q: What is the main difference between a data lake and a warehouse?
flashcards.a: A lake stores every kind of raw data cheaply and fixes the shape at read time. A warehouse cleans and arranges data before storing it.
flashcards.more: A lake usually keeps Parquet, JSON, images and logs in object storage. It's flexible and cheap, but without organization it becomes a messy "data swamp". A warehouse costs more but is clean and fast.

flashcards.q: What is a lakehouse?
flashcards.a: A way to add table structure, transactions and SQL on top of a lake's cheap files, so you get a warehouse's benefits.
flashcards.more: Formats like Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg add a metadata layer over the files. That lets BI reports and ML both run on the same data, with no separate copy needed.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between ETL and ELT?
flashcards.a: ETL transforms first and loads after. ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse with SQL.
flashcards.more: In ELT the raw data stays intact, so if a transformation rule is wrong you can rebuild. Modern cloud warehouses have made ELT cheap and fast. Data is usually arranged in three layers: raw, staging, mart.

flashcards.q: What does a watermark do in an incremental extract?
flashcards.a: It marks how far data was last taken (such as an `updated_at` value), so the next run picks up only new rows.
flashcards.more: The watermark moves only after the file has been written and loaded successfully. Using `>=` brings some duplicates but loses no rows; the staging layer keeps the newest row per id. To catch DELETEs you need soft delete or CDC.

flashcards.q: In ELT, how do the extracted files get into the warehouse?
flashcards.a: The extract writes a file to the lake, then the warehouse's own bulk load (BigQuery `LOAD DATA`, Snowflake or Redshift `COPY`) copies it into the raw table.
flashcards.more: A bulk load is far cheaper and faster than inserting rows one by one from PHP. It appends, so loading a file twice duplicates rows; staging removes them. Run the load before moving the watermark, so a failed load is simply retried.

flashcards.q: What do the staging and mart layers each do?
flashcards.a: Staging removes duplicates (newest row per id). The mart applies the business definition once, such as paid orders by New York day.
flashcards.more: Raw is never edited, so you can rebuild staging and the mart from it if a rule changes. Every dashboard reads the mart, which is how one metric stops having three numbers.

flashcards.q: When should you use batch and when streaming?
flashcards.a: Batch when data that is hours or a day old is fine; streaming when you must act the moment an event happens.
flashcards.more: Batch is simple, cheap and easy to rerun. Streaming is fast but you have to handle ordering, duplicates and late events. Most reports are fine with batch, so start there.

flashcards.q: What are the three core parts of data governance?
flashcards.a: An owner (who is responsible), quality (automatic checks) and a catalog (a list of datasets with definitions).
flashcards.more: Without an owner, nobody is accountable for mistakes. Without quality checks, bad data flows quietly to dashboards. Without a catalog, everyone builds their own copy, and one metric gets three numbers.
